concept.centerRule: A Scene belongs when a bounded source materially requests, announces, withholds, authorizes, interprets, or embodies forgiveness, pardon, remission, covered or uncounted sin, or remembered-no-more language. Shared vocabulary never erases speaker, wrong, authority, condition, means, consequence, or uncertainty.

characterAnchors.label: Joseph
characterAnchors.note: Answers his brothers’ pardon request with tears, Godward restraint, provision, and comfort without an explicit pardon formula.

characterAnchors.label: Moses
characterAnchors.note: Asks pardon after the calf and appeals to the proclaimed divine character when Israel faces judgment.

characterAnchors.label: Saul
characterAnchors.note: Admits sin and asks Samuel to pardon and return after rejected kingship is announced.

characterAnchors.label: David
characterAnchors.note: Receives Abigail’s pardon request while being turned away from planned bloodshed.

characterAnchors.label: Solomon
characterAnchors.note: Builds repeated hear-and-forgive petitions into the Temple dedication prayer.

characterAnchors.label: Job
characterAnchors.note: Asks why his disobedience is not pardoned before death, without receiving an answer inside the Scene.

characterAnchors.label: Isaiah
characterAnchors.note: Moves from unclean lips through removed guilt and forgiven sin to volunteered sending.

characterAnchors.label: Jeremiah
characterAnchors.note: Announces promised forgiveness and also voices a personal request that opponents not be forgiven.

characterAnchors.label: Jesus Christ
characterAnchors.note: Announces forgiveness, teaches prayer and repeated forgiveness, warns about retained sin, and asks forgiveness during crucifixion.

characterAnchors.label: Paul
characterAnchors.note: Proclaims remission through Jesus and directs communities toward forgiveness, comfort, and reconciliation.

concept.throughline: The trail moves from family requests and priestly formulas through intercession, Temple prayer, praise, withheld pardon, prophetic promise, Jesus’ authority and warnings, apostolic proclamation, mutual forgiveness, covenant blood, confession, and remembered-no-more language.

edges.basis: Both scenes begin with a request, but one response comforts without a pardon formula and the other is followed by renewed refusal. Joseph’s brothers request forgiveness for their evil, while Joseph weeps, refuses God’s place, distinguishes intentions, promises provision, and comforts them without an explicit “I forgive you” formula. Pharaoh confesses, asks forgiveness and prayer, receives relief, and again refuses release when his heart is hardened.
edges.label: The brothers ask; Joseph answers without a pardon formula · Pharaoh asks forgiveness and returns to refusal

edges.basis: One source warns that the named messenger will not pardon provocation; the other records Moses asking for forgiveness after the calf. The promised messenger carries the divine name and a warning that provocation will not be pardoned. Moses asks whether Israel’s calf sin may be forgiven and offers his own erasure, while the reply distinguishes the sinner, continued guidance, and future punishment.
edges.label: The messenger bears the name and will not pardon provocation · Moses asks pardon after the calf

edges.basis: The proclamation joins forgiveness and not clearing; Numbers later narrates explicit pardon alongside a retained wilderness consequence. The proclaimed divine name joins abundant covenant love and forgiving sin with refusal to clear guilt and generational visitation before Moses asks for pardon and inheritance. Repeated sin-offering cases identify offender, offering, priestly atonement, and the stated result that the person or assembly is forgiven.
edges.label: The proclaimed name forgives and does not clear · Sin-offering cases end with “forgiven”

edges.basis: Both legal units end in forgiveness, while confession, economic ability, restitution, offering, and priestly action differ. Confession, graded offerings, restitution, ignorance, priestly atonement, and forgiveness are distinguished across several cases. Deception, robbery, lost property, restitution with an added fifth, a guilt offering, atonement, and forgiveness appear in one procedure.
edges.label: Confession, graded offerings, and forgiveness · Restitution precedes offering and forgiveness

edges.basis: One unit separates unintentional from high-handed action; the other treats a vow made void by household authority. Moses appeals to the proclaimed divine character, the LORD states that the people are pardoned, and the unbelieving generation still receives a wilderness sentence. Congregational and individual unintentional wrongs receive atonement and forgiveness, while high-handed action is distinguished and cut off.
edges.label: Israel is pardoned and still sentenced · Forgiveness for error; a boundary for defiance

edges.basis: Deuteronomy supplies a communal request where culpability is unknown and denies pardon where a person knowingly persists. Vows made void by a father or husband are followed by repeated statements that the LORD will forgive the woman. An unresolved murder leads to elders, sacrifice, washing, confession of nonparticipation, a request for forgiveness, and removal of innocent blood.
edges.label: Voided vows are followed by forgiveness · An unresolved murder leads to a pardon request

edges.basis: The people promise service under a no-forgiveness warning; Saul asks pardon after rejected kingship has been announced. The covenant warning says the LORD will not pardon the person who privately blesses himself while persisting in idolatrous refusal. Joshua’s covenant warning says the holy and jealous God will not forgive rebellion and sin, while the people repeatedly promise service.
edges.label: Private self-assurance meets “will not pardon” · Joshua warns that rebellion will not be forgiven

edges.basis: Abigail asks pardon while interrupting one planned killing; Solomon prays for future persons, communities, foreigners, and exiles. Saul admits sin and asks Samuel to pardon and return, but rejected kingship, public worship, and Samuel’s response remain distinct. Abigail asks David to forgive her trespass while interrupting planned bloodshed; David blesses her discernment and accepts the gift.
edges.label: Saul asks pardon after kingship is rejected · Abigail asks forgiveness and interrupts bloodshed

edges.basis: One scene preserves an ambiguous peaceful response; the other supplies a narrator explanation for national collapse. Solomon’s Temple prayer repeatedly asks God to hear and forgive across personal dispute, defeat, drought, disaster, war, foreign prayer, and exile. Naaman anticipates bowing in Rimmon’s house, asks pardon, and receives Elisha’s “Go in peace” without a narrated explanation of the request.
edges.label: Solomon asks God to hear and forgive · Naaman asks pardon and hears “Go in peace”

edges.basis: One covenant response gives a public sequence; one narrative reports intercession and healing for participants outside the written order. Jerusalem’s collapse is related to Manasseh’s sins and innocent blood with the statement that the LORD would not pardon. God’s answer to Solomon joins humility, prayer, seeking, turning, hearing, forgiveness, healing, covenant warning, and exile from the land.
edges.label: Jerusalem falls after “would not pardon” · Humility, prayer, turning, forgiveness, and healing

edges.basis: A communal prayer praises repeated patience; an individual lament asks why pardon has not come before death. Uncleansed Passover participants eat contrary to the written rule; Hezekiah asks pardon, the LORD hears, and the people are healed. The communal prayer recounts repeated rebellion and describes God as ready to pardon, gracious, merciful, patient, and unwilling to forsake.
edges.label: Hezekiah asks pardon for irregular Passover worship · The prayer remembers a God ready to pardon

edges.basis: One speaker petitions amid affliction and waiting; another recounts concealment, confession, forgiveness, and joy. Job asks why his disobedience is not pardoned before he lies down in the dust, preserving complaint rather than an announced divine response. The speaker asks pardon for great iniquity and forgiveness of all sins amid guidance, covenant love, enemies, affliction, and waiting.
edges.label: Job asks why he is not pardoned · The speaker asks pardon for great iniquity

edges.basis: Both poems remember pardon and turned anger while preserving continued unbelief or a renewed appeal. Forgiven disobedience and covered sin are narrated through silence, bodily distress, confession, divine forgiveness, instruction, and joy. Continuing unbelief and deceptive return stand beside repeated mercy, forgiven iniquity, restrained anger, and remembered mortality.
edges.label: Silence gives way to confession and forgiven sin · Repeated mercy meets continued unbelief

edges.basis: Psalm 99 retains punitive action; Psalm 103 praises removed transgression and remembered frailty. Restoration, forgiven iniquity, covered sin, turned wrath, renewed appeal, covenant love, righteousness, peace, and future good are held together. The LORD answers, forgives, and also takes vengeance for deeds within a psalm of holy kingship and remembered mediators.
edges.label: Forgiven iniquity opens into another appeal · God forgave and took vengeance for deeds

edges.basis: Psalm 130 moves toward fear and waiting; Isaiah 6 moves from removed guilt to volunteered sending. Forgiveness, healing, redemption, mercy, justice, compassion, removed transgression, and remembered human frailty appear in one praise sequence. The depths prayer places marked iniquity beside forgiveness, fear, waiting, covenant love, abundant redemption, and Israel’s hope.
edges.label: Forgiveness is praised beside removed transgression and remembered frailty · Forgiveness stands so that God may be feared

edges.basis: One oracle closes a present refusal with death; another pictures a secure city whose people are forgiven.
